warmup.q: A request thread calls future.get(200, MILLISECONDS) on a task that charges a card. The issuer takes 600 ms, so get throws TimeoutException. What happens to the charge?
options: It is cancelled, because the timeout cancels the task
It keeps going, and the card is charged about 400 ms later
It is rolled back when TimeoutException is thrown
The task gets a TimeoutException too and stops
warmup.why: A timeout ends your wait, not the task. Nothing tells the task you gave up, so it finishes and the issuer approves the charge. To stop it you must call cancel(true), and even that only sends an interrupt the task may or may not notice in time.

sections.h: Callable returns a value, and Future is the claim ticket
sections.html:
Runnable.run() returns nothing and can't throw checked exceptions. Callable<V>.call() returns a V and may throw any Exception, which makes it the natural shape for "call the issuer and give me the answer". Hand one to submit and you get a Future<V> back at once, a claim ticket for a result that doesn't exist yet:

Java
Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment));   // returns at once
String decision = auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);              // waits up to 200 ms
Kotlin
val auth: Future<String> = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment) }  // returns at once
val decision = auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                          // waits up to 200 ms

get() blocks until the task finishes. Then it returns the value, or throws ExecutionException with the task's exception as the cause, or CancellationException if the task was cancelled. It throws InterruptedException if your own thread is interrupted while it waits. A successful get() also gives you visibility: everything the task wrote before it finished is visible to the thread that got the result.

Use get(timeout, unit) in request paths. Plain get() waits forever, and forever is how one slow dependency turns into a pile of hung request threads.

You can also submit a plain Runnable. The Future<?> you get back returns null from get(), which is still useful: it tells you when the task finished and whether it threw.

The part people miss is that a timeout ends your wait, not the task. TimeoutDemo shows it:

  16 ms  pool-1-thread-1 calling the issuer
 216 ms  main         get timed out after 200 ms
 648 ms  pool-1-thread-1 issuer answered: APPROVED (and the charge went through)

The caller gave up at 200 ms and probably told the customer the payment failed. The task kept going, and the issuer approved the charge 430 ms later. So when you stop waiting, decide what happens to the work: cancel it, or make sure its result still gets recorded somewhere a retry can find it.

try.title: Give up on a slow issuer
steps: Run TimeoutDemo (either language). Note the time on the issuer answered line.
Run it again with -Pargs=cancel, which calls cancel(true) after the timeout. Predict: does the issuer still answer?

code.title: TimeoutDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** get(200 ms) on a call that takes 600 ms. Pass "cancel" to cancel(true) after the timeout. */ public class TimeoutDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-12s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean cancel = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> { log("calling the issuer"); try { Thread.sleep(600); // the issuer is slow today } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("interrupted: giving up on the issuer"); throw e; } log("issuer answered: APPROVED (and the charge went through)"); return "APPROVED"; }); try { log("result: " + auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { log("get timed out after 200 ms"); if (cancel) log("cancel(true) returned " + auth.cancel(true)); } } // close() waits for the task, which is still running unless we cancelled it log("pool closed"); } }

alt.title: TimeoutDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %-12s %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().name, msg)) /** get(200 ms) on a call that takes 600 ms. Pass "cancel" to cancel(true) after the timeout. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val cancel = args.firstOrNull() == "cancel" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> val auth = pool.submit<String> { log("calling the issuer") try { Thread.sleep(600) // the issuer is slow today } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("interrupted: giving up on the issuer") throw e } log("issuer answered: APPROVED (and the charge went through)") "APPROVED" } try { log("result: " + auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { log("get timed out after 200 ms") if (cancel) log("cancel(true) returned " + auth.cancel(true)) } } // close() waits for the task, which is still running unless we cancelled it log("pool closed") }

try.expect: Without cancel, the issuer answers at about 650 ms, long after get timed out, and the pool closes only then. With cancel, the task prints "interrupted: giving up on the issuer" at about 215 ms, cancel(true) returns true, and the pool closes at once.

sections.h: cancel(true) sends an interrupt, nothing more
sections.html:
Future.cancel(boolean mayInterruptIfRunning) has two modes. cancel(false) stops a task that hasn't started, so it will never run, and leaves a running task alone. cancel(true) does the same and, if the task is running, calls interrupt() on the thread running it.

That is all it does. Java has no safe way to kill a thread: Thread.stop was deprecated for decades, has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since JDK 20, and was removed in JDK 26. Cancellation is cooperative. An interrupt sets a flag on the thread. If the thread is blocked in a method that responds to interrupts (Thread.sleep, Object.wait, BlockingQueue.take, Future.get and others), that method wakes up and throws InterruptedException. Code that never blocks and never checks the flag doesn't notice anything.

CancelDemo cancels three tasks 100 ms after they start:

after cancel: isCancelled=true/true/true isDone=true/true/true
sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping
checker: saw the flag after 46 slices, stopping
ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway

Read the first line again. All three futures report cancelled and done straight away. A Future changes state the moment you call cancel. It doesn't wait for the task to stop. The ignorer then ran to the end. If its work was posting to a ledger, the post happened, and the Future still says cancelled.

Two rules follow. A long CPU loop should check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() every so often, as the checker does. And a cancelled Future only tells you that nobody will get a result from it. It does not tell you the side effects didn't happen.

cancel(false) has its own use. During a graceful shutdown you may want running settlements to finish but queued ones never to start: cancel the queued futures with false and let awaitTermination wait for the rest. cancel returns false if the task had already finished or was already cancelled, which tells you the cancel came too late.

try.title: Cancel three kinds of task
steps: Run CancelDemo and match each line of output to one of the three tasks.
Make the ignorer cooperate: add the same isInterrupted() check the checker has at the top of its loop. Predict how long the demo takes now, then run it.

code.title: CancelDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** cancel(true) on three tasks: one that sleeps, one that checks the flag, one that never looks. */ public class CancelDemo { // about a second of CPU work, in slices static long slice(long x) { for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) x = x * 31 + i; return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { Future<?> sleeper = pool.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(5_000); System.out.println("sleeper: woke up normally"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping"); } }); Future<?> checker = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { System.out.println("checker: saw the flag after " + s + " slices, stopping"); return; } x = slice(x); } System.out.println("checker: finished all slices " + (x & 1)); }); Future<?> ignorer = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) x = slice(x); // never looks at the flag System.out.println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway " + (x & 1)); }); Thread.sleep(100); for (Future<?> f : new Future<?>[] {sleeper, checker, ignorer}) f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b%n", sleeper.isCancelled(), checker.isCancelled(), ignorer.isCancelled(), sleeper.isDone(), checker.isDone(), ignorer.isDone()); } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU System.out.println("pool closed"); } }

alt.title: CancelDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Executors // about a second of CPU work, in slices private fun slice(start: Long): Long { var x = start for (i in 0 until 2_000_000) x = x * 31 + i return x } /** cancel(true) on three tasks: one that sleeps, one that checks the flag, one that never looks. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> val sleeper = pool.submit { try { Thread.sleep(5_000) println("sleeper: woke up normally") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping") } } val checker = pool.submit { var x = 0L for (s in 0 until 400) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { println("checker: saw the flag after $s slices, stopping") return@submit } x = slice(x) } println("checker: finished all slices ${x and 1}") } val ignorer = pool.submit { var x = 0L repeat(400) { x = slice(x) } // never looks at the flag println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway ${x and 1}") } Thread.sleep(100) listOf(sleeper, checker, ignorer).forEach { it.cancel(true) } println("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b".format( sleeper.isCancelled, checker.isCancelled, ignorer.isCancelled, sleeper.isDone, checker.isDone, ignorer.isDone)) } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU println("pool closed") }

try.expect: First run: the sleeper and the checker stop within milliseconds, but the ignorer burns about a second of CPU and close() waits for it, so "pool closed" comes last. After your change the ignorer stops after a few dozen slices too, and the demo finishes in well under a second after the cancel.

sections.h: The interruption protocol: rethrow or restore
sections.html:
When a blocking method throws InterruptedException, it clears the thread's interrupt flag first. That one detail is behind most interrupt bugs. If you catch the exception and carry on, the request to stop is gone, and no code further up can see it.

Here is how that bites. A helper sleeps between polls and swallows the exception, because "there's nothing useful to do here". The loop around it checks isInterrupted() correctly and still never stops, because the helper cleared the flag before the loop could look at it. That is the bug in the lab's StatementPoller, and neither shutdownNow() nor cancel(true) can stop it.

The Thread Javadoc in JDK 26 states the rule in a new section on interruption: code that catches InterruptedException should rethrow it, or restore the interrupted status with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before it continues or throws something else. So there are two correct moves:

Java
// 1. propagate: declare it and let it go up
void settle(Batch b) throws InterruptedException {
    ledgerQueue.put(b);
}

// 2. you can't propagate (Runnable.run can't throw it): restore the flag
public void run() {
    try {
        ledgerQueue.put(batch);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // keep the request visible
        return;                               // and stop
    }
}
Kotlin
// 1. propagate: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so simply don't catch it
fun settle(b: Batch) {
    ledgerQueue.put(b)
}

// 2. if you do catch it: restore the flag
override fun run() {
    try {
        ledgerQueue.put(batch)
    } catch (e: InterruptedException) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt()    // keep the request visible
        return                                // and stop
    }
}

Wrapping is fine if you restore the flag first: catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new LedgerUnavailableException(e); }. Logging it and moving on is not.

One more trap: whether a blocked network read notices an interrupt depends on the API. NIO channels (the java.nio.channels API) do: the JDK closes the channel and the read fails. A classic java.net.Socket stream read on a platform thread does not. Give every HTTP and database client its own timeout, and treat the interrupt as a second line of defence.

Check yourself: a task catches InterruptedException from Thread.sleep, logs it, and loops back to sleep again. Does the second sleep throw at once? No. The flag was cleared when the first exception was thrown, so the second sleep waits its full time. Add Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to the catch and the second sleep throws immediately, because sleep checks the flag before it starts to wait.

Before JDK 19, asking a Future how it ended meant calling get() inside a try with three catch blocks. JDK 19 added state(), which never blocks, and two accessors for futures you already know are done:

Java
switch (f.state()) {
    case RUNNING   -> log.info("still waiting on the issuer");
    case SUCCESS   -> record(f.resultNow());                   // the value, no checked exceptions
    case FAILED    -> log.warn("issuer failed", f.exceptionNow());  // the task's own exception, unwrapped
    case CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled");
}
Kotlin
when (f.state()) {
    Future.State.RUNNING -> log.info("still waiting on the issuer")
    Future.State.SUCCESS -> record(f.resultNow())              // the value, no checked exceptions
    Future.State.FAILED -> log.warn("issuer failed", f.exceptionNow())  // the task's own exception, unwrapped
    Future.State.CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled")
}

resultNow() throws IllegalStateException if the task isn't done or didn't succeed. exceptionNow() throws it if the task didn't fail, including when it was cancelled. Call them after checking state(), or on futures you know are finished.

ExecutorService also has two bulk methods. invokeAll(tasks) runs every task and returns their futures once all are done. With a timeout, it cancels whatever hasn't finished by the deadline, so every future it returns is done. invokeAny(tasks) returns the result of the first task that succeeds, cancels the rest, and throws ExecutionException only if every task fails. That fits "ask three FX-rate providers and take the first good answer".

In InvokeAnyDemo the fastest provider fails after 100 ms. invokeAny ignores that failure, returns the answer from the provider that succeeds at 200 ms, and interrupts the slowest. invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline returns one future of each kind: failed, succeeded and cancelled.

Both bulk methods block the calling thread until they return, so call them from a thread that may wait, never from a task running on the same bounded pool. A pool of 3 whose tasks each call invokeAll with 3 subtasks on that pool can end up with every thread waiting for subtasks that have no thread to run on. Lesson 9 of this track calls that pool-induced deadlock.

try.title: First answer wins
steps: Read the three providers in InvokeAnyDemo: alpha takes 300 ms, beta fails at 100 ms, gamma takes 200 ms. Predict what invokeAny returns and which provider gets interrupted.
Predict the three states invokeAll reports with its 250 ms deadline, then run the demo.

code.title: InvokeAnyDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ public class InvokeAnyDemo { static Callable<String> provider(String name, long millis, boolean fails) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(millis); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": interrupted, cancelled"); throw e; } if (fails) throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is down"); return name + " EUR/USD 1.0842"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { List<Callable<String>> providers = List.of( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false)); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { System.out.println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:"); List<Future<String>> all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); for (Future<String> f : all) { System.out.println(" " + f.state() + switch (f.state()) { case SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow(); case FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().getMessage(); default -> ""; }); } } } }

alt.title: InvokeAnyDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Future import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private fun provider(name: String, millis: Long, fails: Boolean) = Callable { try { Thread.sleep(millis) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println(" $name: interrupted, cancelled") throw e } if (fails) throw IllegalStateException("$name is down") "$name EUR/USD 1.0842" } /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ fun main() { val providers = listOf( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false), ) Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)) Thread.sleep(50) println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:") val all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) for (f in all) { val detail = when (f.state()) { Future.State.SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow() Future.State.FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().message else -> "" } println(" ${f.state()}$detail") } } }

try.expect: invokeAny returns gamma's rate: beta finished first but failed, and a failure doesn't count. Alpha prints "interrupted, cancelled". With the 250 ms deadline, invokeAll reports alpha CANCELLED (interrupted at the deadline), beta FAILED with "beta is down" and gamma SUCCESS.

refs.title: ExecutorService (Java SE 25 API): invokeAll and invokeAny

analogy: A Future is the ticket from a dry cleaner. You can come back and wait at the counter (get), wait only until your lunch break ends (get with a timeout), or ask the shop how your shirt is doing without waiting (state). Cancelling is phoning the shop to say "don't bother". If they haven't started, the shirt never gets cleaned. If it is already in the machine, the clerk may or may not hear the phone, and either way your ticket now says "cancelled". The analogy breaks at the end: a real shop tells you whether the shirt got cleaned. A cancelled Future never tells you whether the work happened.
world: Every call your payment service makes to an issuer, a fraud scorer or a ledger API should have a deadline, and a timeout should lead somewhere on purpose. For an authorization, "we stopped waiting" is not "declined": return a pending status, keep the idempotency key, and let a reconciler ask the issuer what happened. In a Kafka consumer, a stuck downstream call that ignores interrupts blocks the partition and, through max.poll.interval.ms, eventually costs you the partition. In the Temporal Java SDK, an activity learns it was cancelled when it heartbeats, so an activity stuck in one long blocking call with no timeout of its own never finds out. And grep for catch (InterruptedException e) in your services: every one should rethrow or restore the flag.
mistake: Catching InterruptedException and carrying on, usually in a helper like sleepQuietly() or in a retry loop that "just tries again". It happens because the compiler forces a catch in Java, and the quickest way to make it compile is an empty block. The flag is cleared when the exception is thrown, so the stop request vanishes and shutdownNow() or cancel(true) silently stop working. Fix: propagate it, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() in the catch and then stop or throw.

compare.title: Cancelling work: Future and interrupts vs coroutine cancellation

java.title: CancelOne.java
java.html: Future<String> f = pool.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(5_000); // wakes with InterruptedException on cancel(true) return "done"; }); Thread.sleep(100); f.cancel(true); // sends an interrupt to the worker thread // f.isCancelled() is true at once, whatever the task does next

kotlin.title: CancelOne.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(5_000) // suspends; resumes with CancellationException on cancel println("done") } delay(100) job.cancel() // no interrupt: delay() notices the cancellation itself // a blocking call ignores job.cancel() unless you wrap it: // runInterruptible { Thread.sleep(5_000) }

compare.note: Both models are cooperative, and both need the task to listen. Java delivers the request as a thread interrupt, which blocking methods and isInterrupted() checks pick up. Coroutines deliver it as a CancellationException at suspension points such as delay, await and withContext, with no interrupt at all, so a blocking Java call inside a coroutine doesn't notice unless you wrap it in runInterruptible. The interrupt rules from this lesson still apply to Kotlin code that runs blocking work on an executor. Watch runCatching there: it catches InterruptedException like any other exception, which makes it an easy way to swallow a stop request.

worked.title: Give up on a slow issuer without lying to the customer

steps.say: An authorization handler submits the issuer call to a pool and waits for it. Under normal load this works. What happens when the issuer starts taking 30 seconds?
steps.code: Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment)); return auth.get(); // waits as long as the issuer does

alt.html: val auth = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment) } return auth.get() // waits as long as the issuer does

steps.say: Every request thread ends up parked in get(). Little's law from lesson 3 of this track does the rest: at 400 requests a second and 30 s each, you would need 12,000 threads. The service stops answering anything. Bound the wait, and cancel the work you stopped waiting for.
steps.code: Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment)); try { return auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // 1. bounded wait } catch (TimeoutException e) { auth.cancel(true); // 2. interrupt the issuer call return "PENDING"; // 3. don't claim it was declined }

alt.html: val auth = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment) } return try { auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. bounded wait } catch (e: TimeoutException) { auth.cancel(true) // 2. interrupt the issuer call "PENDING" // 3. don't claim it was declined }

steps.say: Why PENDING and not DECLINED? The interrupt may arrive after the request already reached the issuer, and a classic socket read may not even notice it. The charge can still happen. Saying "declined" invites the customer to pay again, and then you have a double charge.

Make the outcome findable. Send an idempotency key with the request, and on timeout hand the key to a reconciler that asks the issuer later what happened to it. A retry with the same key can't charge twice.
steps.code: String key = payment.idempotencyKey(); Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment, key)); try { return auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { auth.cancel(true); reconciler.checkLater(key); // "what happened to key X?" return "PENDING"; }

alt.html: val key = payment.idempotencyKey() val auth = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment, key) } return try { auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { auth.cancel(true) reconciler.checkLater(key) // "what happened to key X?" "PENDING" }

lab.title: Deadlines, states and a poller that won't stop
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail.
Write Futures.getOrDefault: get with the timeout, and one catch for each outcome in the Javadoc. On timeout and on your own interruption, call cancel(true) first.
Write Futures.describe with a switch on future.state(), using resultNow() and exceptionNow().
StatementPoller is the buggy version. Run its two tests and read the failure: the executor never terminates. Find the line that defeats the loop condition and fix it with one statement.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: get(long, TimeUnit) throws four checked or unchecked exceptions here: TimeoutException, ExecutionException, CancellationException and InterruptedException. A multi-catch handles the two that share an answer.
In getOrDefault, after you cancel on InterruptedException, rethrow the same exception. Propagating it is one of the two correct moves, so you don't also restore the flag.
The poller's while condition is fine. Ask what state the interrupt flag is in when that condition runs right after pause() caught an InterruptedException.

drill.title: A polling loop that stops when asked
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Runnable that calls poll() once a second until the thread is interrupted, then returns. It must stop whether the interrupt arrives during poll() or during the sleep. Then compare. Did you restore the flag, or return straight from the catch?

answer.title: Poller.java
answer.html: Runnable poller = () -> { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { // interrupt during poll(): seen here poll(); try { Thread.sleep(1_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { // interrupt during sleep: flag now cleared Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore it (or simply return) } } };

alt.title: Poller.kt
alt.html: val poller = Runnable { while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { // interrupt during poll(): seen here poll() try { Thread.sleep(1_000) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { // interrupt during sleep: flag now cleared Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // restore it (or simply return) } } }

recap: submit(Callable) returns a Future at once. get returns the value or throws ExecutionException, CancellationException or InterruptedException.
get(timeout) ends your wait, not the task. Cancel the work or make its outcome findable, for example with an idempotency key.
cancel(true) only interrupts. The task stops if it is blocked in an interruptible call or checks isInterrupted(). The Future says cancelled either way.
Throwing InterruptedException clears the flag. Rethrow it or restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). Never swallow it.
JDK 19 added state(), resultNow() and exceptionNow(). invokeAll waits for all, invokeAny returns the first success and cancels the rest.

explain.prompt: A teammate's code has catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted, retrying"); } inside a retry loop. Explain why this breaks shutdown, and what they should write instead.
explain.answer: When a blocking call like sleep or take throws InterruptedException, it clears the thread's interrupt flag. Logging and retrying means the stop request is gone: the loop has no way to know someone asked it to stop. So when the pool calls shutdownNow or someone calls cancel(true), this task just keeps retrying, awaitTermination times out, and the pod gets killed mid-work. They should either let the exception propagate (declare throws InterruptedException), or, if the method can't throw it, call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() in the catch and then stop the loop or throw a different exception. Anything above them that checks the flag then still sees the request.

deeper.html:
Two methods read the interrupt flag and they are easy to mix up. Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() reads it and leaves it alone. The static Thread.interrupted() reads it and clears it. Use the second only when you are about to handle the interrupt yourself, for example to throw InterruptedException from your own blocking method:

Java
if (Thread.interrupted()) throw new InterruptedException();   // clear, then report by throwing
Kotlin
if (Thread.interrupted()) throw InterruptedException()        // clear, then report by throwing

How does cancel(true) find the thread? FutureTask remembers the thread that is running it. cancel(true) moves the task to a cancelled state and then calls interrupt() on that thread. Because the flag belongs to the thread and not to the task, a pool has to make sure an interrupt meant for one task doesn't hit the next one on the same worker. ThreadPoolExecutor does that: before each task, its worker clears any leftover interrupt, unless the pool itself is stopping after shutdownNow().

Virtual threads, in the "Virtual threads" track, use the same interrupt mechanism. A virtual thread blocked in sleep or a BlockingQueue responds exactly as described here, so everything in this lesson carries over.
